Geospatial experiment · Historical traffic

Los Angeles, measured in minutes

In Los Angeles, distance is measured as much in minutes as in miles: a ten-mile trip can take ten minutes or an hour, depending on the time of day. This freeway-mediated cartogram shows how the city expands and contracts through a typical weekday. Choose an origin, move through the five-minute timeline, and compare geography with travel-time geometry.

Median at each five-minute clock time across 85 weekdays · METR-LA, Mar–Jun 2012 · Caltrans PeMS / DCRNN · © OpenStreetMap contributors
Method + assumptions

Historical weekday medians, not live traffic. Routes use the directed freeway graph and eight route-and-direction-diverse entry and exit ramps per catchment. Because this OSM snapshot contains only freeways and ramps, surface access is modeled at 15 mph with 1.25× circuity and a 2.5-minute terminal penalty; tooltips also show a 20 mph optimistic floor. Extreme freeway detours are rejected. Hatching marks sparse geographic coverage; “sensor completeness” only describes the available readings at that clock time. The 3:00 AM outline and minute scale stay fixed while time changes, and within-catchment travel is not modeled.
